doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

chapter: New York Pops and later work
title: Recording quickly today and the first Sinatra sessions
summary: Fast recording for EMI; his first record date with Sinatra paid thirty-five dollars.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: How much time do you get to create an album with the New York Pops in the studio?
I don’t know. Show up and get it over with. I just recorded with a lady from Japan for EMI. I’d never met her, the music didn’t arrive until that morning.

She sang in as we say the native language. So I spent the time looking at her diaphragm, feeling that if I watched her diaphragm I could understand what she was going about. And we did something like four sides in three hours with a big orchestra. It was unbelievable. She’s going to be with me in Tokyo this year. She did this as a preview. But there is no time. Time is gone. It’s gone. That’s a part of technology or part of greed. I don’t know what it is. I began in the record business when we got thirty-five dollars for a date. I made a record with Sinatra, the first record he made I played piano, “Night and Day” and “The Night We Called it a Day,” Axel Stordahl made the arrangements. Eleven or twelve men in the orchestra. And thirty-five dollars, and you took out, I don’t know, there was Social Security, yeah it had started, so I think you ended up with like twenty- eight dollars, this was a big day.
